fixes.explanation: Bethel is a real name, but it's not the one in this verse. The Lord GOD says, "See, I lay a stone in Zion…" So the stone goes in Zion. Hang on to that name, friend.

That's what He says: "the one who believes will never be shaken." It comes right after the tested stone, the precious cornerstone, the sure foundation. I spent years in the back of a junk drawer, so believe me, a foundation that doesn't move sounds GOOD.

Yes, it's False. The Lord GOD says, "Your covenant with death will be dissolved, and your agreement with Sheol will not stand." That covenant is what the rulers said they had made. He says it comes apart.
Not what Isaiah says. He calls it "…His strange work…" and "…His disturbing task." Strange means unusual, and disturbing means unsettling. Easy and expected aren't words you'll find in that verse.

Isaiah's question is, "Does the plowman plow for planting every day?" He's asking it because the answer is no. The next verse says that when he has leveled the surface, he sows caraway and scatters cumin. Plowing all year long? Friend, even I would ask that man if he's okay.

Resting the field isn't what these verses say. Isaiah says, "When he has leveled its surface, does he not sow caraway and scatter cumin?" So the farmer levels the surface, and then he sows. A year off isn't in the picture.

Isaiah says the opposite. "He plants wheat in rows and barley in plots, and rye within its border." Rows, plots and a border, so each crop gets its own spot. One big pile of seed? That farmer would need a miracle and a very patient sorting crew.

Isaiah says, "But caraway is beaten out with a stick, and cumin with a rod." Right before that, he says caraway is not threshed with a sledge. So the sledge stays out of it, and the farmer reaches for a stick.
A winnowing fork never shows up in these verses. Isaiah says, "But caraway is beaten out with a stick, and cumin with a rod." So the caraway gets a stick. Good guess on a farm tool, though.

That's right. Isaiah says, "Grain for bread must be ground, but it is not endlessly threshed." The farmer threshes it, but not endlessly. I'd be thrilled if my kneading ever came with a stopping point like that.
